column4: At Uhud the verse says Allah fulfilled His promise (the source section's root ص د ق) until the believers faltered, disputed, and disobeyed; it stages fulfilled resolve followed by a broken battle effort.
The section's dictionary gloss for الْحُسْنَيَيْنِ is victory or martyrdom; this battle challenge names precisely the two outcomes the hostile waiters must expect.
The verse says a fighter may be killed or prevail, and either way receives a great reward; it gives the section's victory-or-martyrdom gloss of الْحُسْنَىٰ a direct battle setting.
The verse binds wealth and lives to fighting and says believers may kill or be killed, in exchange for Paradise; it joins the section's giving and completed charge to the two good battle outcomes.
The root ص د ق in the source section means carrying a battle effort through; here, amid the Confederates' siege, men have fulfilled the covenant they made with Allah.
This ayah places spending and fighting before or after the conquest under one promise of الْحُسْنَىٰ, joining the section's given hand and sustained battle to a promised good.
The verse joins giving wealth, fulfilling covenants, and patience in hardship and at battle; it gathers the source section's gift, fidelity, and sustained combat into one account of righteousness.

The verse identifies those who hinder fighters, urge their brothers back, come to battle only a little, and are stingy; it concretizes the section's contrast between giving into the fight and breaking off.
At meeting an enemy force, the verse commands believers to stand firm (فَاثْبُتُوا۟); this is the military steadiness behind the section's sound spear and charge carried through.
The fighters stand as a compact structure (بُنْيَانٌ مَّرْصُوصٌ); the source section's dictionary gloss of ص د ق as solid becomes a formation, not only hard iron.
After Uhud, fortunes alternate and Allah takes martyrs from among the believers; this gives the section's shahada outcome a concrete place within a changing battle.
The verse says Allah purifies believers and effaces disbelievers in the continuing Uhud scene; it names a further consequence of the battle that produces the martyrs in 3:140.
The verse asks whether believers expect Paradise before Allah distinguishes those who strive and remain patient; it makes sustained effort in battle the test behind the section's good outcome.
The verse recalls that believers had wished for death before meeting it and then saw it; it gives the section's martyr outcome the moment of facing battle death.
The verse says those killed in Allah's cause are alive and provided for; it explains the martyr side of the section's two good outcomes beyond the battlefield.
The verse recalls fighters beside prophets who did not weaken or submit after hardship; it shows the sustained resolve opposite the section's abandoned charge.
The verse warns that dispute makes a fighting group fail and lose its force; its neighbor 8:45 commands firmness, while this ayah names what breaks it.
Satan promises support when the armies are apart, but when they meet he turns back on his heels (نَكَصَ عَلَىٰ عَقِبَيْهِ); it is a precise battle image of assurance abandoned at the charge.
The hypocrites promise to leave with their allies or help them if attacked, but Allah calls them liars (لَكَاذِبُونَ); this is the source root ك ذ ب applied to a broken battle pledge.
The next ayah says the hypocrites will not leave or help if their allies are attacked, then will turn their backs; it spells out the failure forecast in 59:11.
The source root ص د ق names giving battle its due; this ayah says that after a decision, being true to Allah would be better, while 47:20 shows the fearful response when fighting is mentioned.
The command to march and strive with wealth and lives makes the section's gift and battle effort one joined act.
The verse remembers believers driven from home, harmed, then fighting and being killed; it links hardship, a completed fight, and divine reward to the section's martyr outcome.
The verse names those who migrate in Allah's cause and are killed or die, then promises good provision and a pleasing entry; it develops the section's martyr outcome after combat.
The verse says death in Allah's cause brings forgiveness and mercy better than what people gather; this gives the section's martyrdom outcome a reward that outweighs worldly goods.
When armies meet, this verse describes striking necks before regulating captives; it supplies a concrete Quranic battle scene for the source section's cutting sword.
The command not to turn backs when facing an enemy is the direct battlefield boundary against the back-turning in the source section.
This ayah condemns turning one's back in battle but exempts a tactical maneuver or joining another group; it gives the section's fleeing image both its limit and its grave consequence.
Under siege, some tell the people to return and claim their homes are exposed; the verse says they want only to flee, making the source section's turn-away an explicit wartime retreat.
The opponents are distressed by a good outcome and rejoice at misfortune, then turn away (يَتَوَلَّوا۟); the neighboring 9:52 answers them that believers face only two good battle outcomes.
This ayah says nothing will strike believers except what Allah has decreed and calls them to rely on Him; the next 9:52 names victory or martyrdom as the battle's two goods.
Still within the siege, the verse says the wavering group would comply if attackers pressed them toward fitna; it shows their charge failing under pressure.
The verse recalls their covenant not to turn backs (لَا يُوَلُّونَ الْأَدْبَارَ); the source section's root و ل ي names the opposing act of turning away in battle.
The verse says flight cannot help against death or killing; it makes the section's retreat a futile answer to battlefield danger.
The verse asks who can protect them from Allah if harm is decreed; after 33:16's futile flight, it supplies the limit of the shield or bodily protection named in the section.
During the same siege, some say Allah and His Messenger promised only delusion; this is the battlefield denial set against the pledge-fulfillment of 33:23 and the source section's broken charge.
At Uhud some turned back when the armies met, yet Allah pardoned them; this marks a boundary between a battle retreat and the source section's denier who turns away toward fire.
At Hunayn, believers turned their backs after being impressed by their numbers; this is a concrete battle retreat, distinct from the denier's turn in the source section.
After the retreat in 9:25, Allah sent tranquility upon the Messenger and believers; the neighboring ayah adds restoration after flight and prevents treating every retreat as the same case.
The verse asks whether believers would turn back if Muhammad died or were killed; it connects back-turning to fear of loss in battle and says it cannot harm Allah.
The verse describes people who break covenants repeatedly and then addresses meeting them in war; it contrasts broken pledges with the source section's ص د ق as fulfilled combat effort.

Invited to fight or defend, the hypocrites say they would follow if they knew how to fight, then are described as speaking what is not in their hearts; this is a battle-specific gap between claim and action.
Those left behind are called to fight a powerful people; obedience brings a good reward, while turning away brings punishment, joining combat participation to consequence.
If the disbelievers had fought the believers, they would have turned their backs; it gives the source section's retreat a clear reversal, with the enemy rather than the believer fleeing.
At the pledge under the tree, the verse says whoever fulfills his covenant with Allah receives a great reward; it parallels the source section's completed charge as faithful action.

The source root ج ن ب names the shield at a person's side and being kept aside from fire; this ayah speaks of worshippers' sides (جُنُوبُهُمْ) leaving their beds as they call on God in fear and hope and give from their provision.
The source root ج ن ب also means to keep away: this ayah praises those who avoid false gods (اجْتَنَبُوا۟) and gives them good news, echoing the section's pious person kept away from fire.
This ayah says the Fire calls whoever turned away (تَوَلَّىٰ); it echoes the source root و ل ي and makes the section's back-turning lead directly toward its warned fire.
The next ayah describes that person as one who gathered and hoarded (فَأَوْعَىٰ); it completes 70:17's picture of the one called by the Fire and opposes the section's giver who hands over.
The command to urge believers to fight and the promise that a small patient group can face a larger one make endurance in battle explicit.
The next ayah eases the ratio because of weakness while retaining the command to endure; it marks a limit to the firmness demanded in 8:65.
The verse says true believers do not ask to stay behind from striving with wealth and lives; it contrasts the source section's steadfast giver with those who hold back.
The people left behind rejoice at staying home and dislike striving with wealth and lives; this is the refusal to enter the campaign that precedes the section's image of a charge abandoned.
When a fighting passage is revealed, the sick-hearted look at the Messenger as if overcome by death; this gives the source section's failed charge a specific image of fear.

The ayah calls people to spend in Allah's cause, names those who withhold, then says turning away (تَتَوَلَّوْا) brings replacement; it joins the source section's giving and turning-away roots to support for the fight.

The verse distinguishes those who sit from those who strive with wealth and lives, while promising good to both and greater rank to the fighters; it clarifies the different weight of entering the struggle.

While one group prays under threat, it must keep its arms (أَسْلِحَتَهُمْ) ready and the other group takes its turn; this parallels the section's weapons-and-shield image without claiming the verse names a shield.
The command to prepare whatever force and cavalry can be mustered is a direct Quranic counterpart to the section's bow, spear, and sword as battle equipment.
The verse records people saying “obedience” and then plotting otherwise; in the passage framed by the command to fight at 4:77, it states the source section's speech-versus-action divide.
The rebuke asks why people say what they do not do; the next battle image in 61:4 carries the source section's point about completing an action beyond verbal affirmation.
This ayah says Allah greatly detests saying what one does not do; its battlefield neighbor 61:4 turns the source section's speech/action contrast into a fighting formation.
The fearful men are stingy during danger but use sharp tongues (أَلْسِنَةٍ حِدَادٍ) after fear passes; by analogy, it contrasts verbal sharpness with the section's effective, sustained weapon action.
The continuation says that if the confederates returned, these people would fight only a little; it completes 33:18's picture of those who barely enter battle.

By analogy only, the verse pairs humility toward believers with might toward disbelievers and explicitly mentions fighting; its directed qualities resemble the section's hard and yielding iron, though it describes people rather than weapons.
By analogy only, the companions are severe toward disbelievers and merciful among themselves; that contrast resembles the section's hard and yielding materials, though this is not a weapons scene.

The source section names a shield as a side-protector; here oaths are made a shield (جُنَّة) that blocks people from Allah's path, a reversed and figurative use of protection rather than the same root.

The connection is thematic, not a battle scene: the next ayah says wealth and children cannot avail the people just described and assigns them to the Fire, echoing the source section's wider surah context where wealth fails and fire follows denial.
The section's shield is physical protection, while this ayah makes oaths a shield (جُنَّة) for people who obstruct Allah's path; the connection is a specific metaphorical reversal, not a shared root.
Outside a battle scene, the next ayah says these people believed and then disbelieved; it follows the false shield in 63:2 and parallels the source section's denier who turns away.

The source dictionary form is رُمْحٌ صِدْقٌ, a sound spear; 5:94 names spears (رِمَاحُكُمْ) in a hunting test, not a battle. This limited boundary reading shows the weapon's force held back where restraint is required.

The section's dictionary scene makes iron the hardest metal and sharp sword material; this ayah says iron holds formidable power and benefits for people, connecting the weapon metal to strength used in support of God's messengers.
The source section calls masculine iron the hardest; here Allah softens iron for David (وَأَلَنَّا لَهُ الْحَدِيدَ), a specific reversal showing iron can be made yielding for a different use.
The next ayah turns the softened iron of 34:10 into coats of mail and asks for measured links; it gives the section's iron and shield image a Quranic defensive use.
This ayah says God taught David to make armor protecting people from their violence; it repeats the shield side of the section's image in an explicit battle setting.
The section's hard iron is a weapon in battle; this ayah places iron maces (مَقَامِعُ مِنْ حَدِيدٍ) in the Fire, turning the metal into punishment for those who rejected the truth.
The battle command to strike above the necks and at fingertips gives the section's cutting sword a direct Quranic combat scene.
At Badr, the verse says the Prophet did not throw when he threw, but Allah threw; this qualifies the section's image of a completed human charge by locating the battle's effect under divine action.

The verse says Medina's people and nearby Arabs should not stay behind the Messenger or prefer their own lives over his; it directly opposes the section's retreating fighter and self-protective stance.
The next ayah records every small or large expenditure and every valley crossed for the campaign; it makes the section's gift and completed action count even without naming victory.

This ayah says believers should not all go forth together and describes a group learning and warning others; it is a limited boundary to 9:120's wartime call, since the exact division of who travels and who stays is not wholly clear from memory.

The three left behind from Tabuk are eventually forgiven after recognizing they had no refuge from Allah; this is a specific case of repentance after staying behind, unlike the source section's denier who turns toward Fire.

Following the account of those left behind, this ayah commands believers to be with the truthful (الصَّادِقِينَ); it brings the source root ص د ق into the same campaign's question of who truly follows through.
After the people who stayed behind disliked the campaign in 9:81, this ayah says they will not be allowed to go out or fight alongside the Messenger again; it gives refusal a concrete consequence.

The Israelites tell Moses to go fight while they remain seated (إِنَّا هَٰهُنَا قَاعِدُونَ); this is a direct refusal to enter the battle that contrasts with the section's fighter who completes a charge.
When fighting is prescribed, most of the Israelites turn away except a few; the ayah is a direct Quranic example of a call to fight broken off before the charge.
Facing Goliath's army, the believers ask Allah to pour patience on them and make their feet firm; it gives the section's steadfast battle effort a specific prayer.
The next ayah records David killing Goliath and the opposing force being defeated by Allah's permission; it supplies victory as the result of the stand prayed for in 2:250.

At Uhud, two groups among the believers were close to losing heart (تَفْشَلَا), though Allah was their protector; it shows a near-break in the charge that stopped short of the flight in the source image.
The Uhud scene shows believers climbing without looking back while the Messenger calls them from behind; this supplies a literal battlefield back-turning and its immediate grief.

Those who stayed behind claim their advice would have prevented their brothers' deaths; the verse challenges them to repel death if they are truthful (صَادِقِينَ), joining the source root ص د ق to the battle's two outcomes.

After being wounded, believers answer Allah and the Messenger's call to pursue; this is a specific case of resuming the effort after pain, with a great reward promised to those who do good and fear God.
The warning that an enemy force had gathered only increases believers' faith and reliance; this neighboring ayah adds their response to intimidation after they had answered the call in 3:172.
The next ayah says they returned with grace and bounty and no harm touched them; it adds an uninjured return as the outcome of the pursuit in 3:172.

When believers see the Confederates, they say this is what Allah and His Messenger promised and that Allah and His Messenger spoke truly (وَصَدَقَ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ); this is the opposite battlefield stance to the deniers in 33:12.
The next ayah says Allah will reward the truthful for their truth (الصَّادِقِينَ بِصِدْقِهِمْ) and deal with hypocrites; it states the outcome of the fulfilled covenant in 33:23.

The continuation says Allah sent the disbelievers back in rage without gain and spared the believers battle; it supplies the enemy's retreat as a battlefield reversal after the faithful stance in 33:23.
This ayah calls those who believe without doubt and strive with wealth and lives in Allah's cause the truthful (الصَّادِقُونَ); it directly joins the source root ص د ق to completed combat action.
The ayah opens with a trade that saves from painful punishment; the next verse defines that trade as belief and striving with wealth and lives, echoing the section's gift-and-battle exchange.
The verse defines the saving trade as believing in Allah and His Messenger and striving with wealth and lives; it states the section's giving and combat effort in one proposition.
The next ayah promises forgiveness, gardens, and a good dwelling for the fighters of 61:11; it supplies the afterlife reward alongside the section's victory-or-martyrdom outcome.
The ayah adds a nearer victory and conquest believers love (نَصْرٌ مِّنَ اللَّهِ وَفَتْحٌ قَرِيبٌ); after 61:11's spending and striving, it gives a concrete victory-side outcome.
This ayah promises help and firm feet to those who support Allah; it names the steadiness in battle that the section embodies through a sound spear and completed charge.
The command not to weaken or call for peace while superior (وَلَا تَهِنُوا۟ وَتَدْعُوا۟ إِلَى السَّلْمِ) directly sets a boundary against stopping an ongoing battle effort.
The verse tells believers not to weaken in pursuing the enemy; even if they suffer, the enemy suffers too, while they hope in Allah, extending the section's charge through hardship.
When given favor, a person turns away and draws aside with his flank (بِجَانِبِهِ); this repeats the source root ج ن ب's side image alongside the turn-away stance of the self-sufficient man.
This ayah repeats the person who turns aside with his flank after favor (بِجَانِبِهِ); the recurring side-image gives the source section's shield-at-the-flank dictionary sense a contrary use.

Disbelievers spend wealth to block Allah's path, are then defeated, and are gathered to Hell; this reverses the section's giving for a good battle outcome into expenditure that fails and ends in Fire.
The next ayah after the martyrs are called alive and provided for says they rejoice in Allah's bounty and have no fear; it expands the section's shahada outcome into joy without fear.
The following ayah says the martyrs rejoice in Allah's grace and that He does not waste the believers' reward; it completes the post-battle reward passage begun in 3:169.
